title: Rubick: Exploiting Job Reconfigurability for Deep Learning Cluster Scheduling
problem: Existing DL cluster schedulers treat training jobs as black boxes with static execution plans, causing mismatches between execution plans and available resources that lead to poor training performance and cluster underutilization.
method: Rubick co-optimizes job execution planning and resource allocation jointly. Key components: (1) Performance model with 7 fittable parameters capturing GPU, CPU, bandwidth, and strategy-specific behaviors for forward/backward/optimizer phases with overlap modeling. Model is fitted from 7 sampled profiling runs and updated online. (2) Resource sensitivity curves showing throughput vs resource allocation for each job, with best execution plan chosen per allocation. (3) Scheduling algorithm that allocates based on sensitivity curve slopes, shrinking the least-sensitive job to resource the most-sensitive, guaranteeing SLOs via minimum-resource enforcement.

title: Hybrid SLC-MLC RRAM Mixed-Signal Processing-in-Memory Architecture for Transformer Acceleration via Gradient Redistribution
problem: Analog RRAM PIM using multi-level cells (MLC) can offer 2x storage density and higher compute throughput than single-level cells (SLC), but MLC's non-linearity causes catastrophic accuracy degradation (e.g., 40% drop) in Transformer models, while brute-force hybrid SLC/MLC mapping fails to move enough weights into MLC to yield meaningful efficiency gains.
method: HyFlexPIM uses a three-tier mixed-signal RRAM PIM architecture: (1) digital SLC RRAM PIM for attention Q·K^T and ×V operations that require high precision and write real-time vectors, (2) analog SLC RRAM PIM for the most critical static weight rows, and (3) analog MLC RRAM PIM (2-bit per cell) for the error-tolerant majority of static weights. A single analog PIM module is reconfigurable between SLC and MLC via a shared 6-b/7-b flexible SAR-ADC that bypasses the MSB comparison in SLC mode, adding less than 1% area/energy overhead. On the software side, gradient redistribution applies SVD to decompose each linear weight matrix, truncates to a hard threshold rank to maintain iso-computational cost, then fine-tunes for 1-3 epochs with AdamW; the fine-tuning process naturally concentrates gradient magnitude into the top 5-10% of singular values, making those rows clearly demarcated as SLC-critical while 90-95% of weights are safely mapped to MLC.

title: Seesaw: High-throughput LLM Inference via Model Re-sharding
problem: A single static parallelization strategy (tensor parallelism or pipeline parallelism) cannot optimally serve both the prefill and decode stages of LLM inference, leaving throughput on the table.
method: Seesaw dynamically re-shards the model between TP for prefill and PP for decode at every stage boundary. KV cache is moved via a tiered buffering scheme: GPU VRAM for active batches and CPU DRAM as an auxiliary store, with asynchronous swap-in/swap-out pipelines. A transition-minimizing scheduler batches multiple requests together so re-sharding occurs less frequently, amortizing the overhead.

title: Resource Analysis of Low-Overhead Transversal Architectures for Reconfigurable Atom Arrays
problem: Fault-tolerant quantum computation on neutral atom arrays using standard lattice-surgery gate schemes requires O(d) syndrome extraction (SE) rounds per logical gate, where d is the code distance, leading to run times of years for large-scale algorithms such as 2048-bit RSA factoring. Existing resource estimates do not account for transversal gates that reduce SE overhead to O(1) rounds per gate, nor do they provide detailed architectural layouts and logical error models for such schemes.
method: The architecture decomposes target quantum algorithms (benchmarked on Shor's 2048-bit factoring) into modular functional units—magic state factories (8T-to-CCZ distillation with |T> cultivation), ripple-carry quantum adders (Cuccaro MAJ/UMA gadgets with CCZ teleportation), and quantum look-up tables (QROM via GHZ-state-assisted CNOT fan-out)—all implemented using surface-code transversal gates with O(1) SE rounds per logical operation and correlated decoding. Atom movement uses direct optical tweezer shuttling with pipelined ancilla measurement to keep moves local and bounded (≤√2·d·l per step). A heuristic logical error model calibrated against MLE decoder simulations characterizes the elevated per-gate noise from transversal CNOTs via a decoding factor α≈1/6. Space-time trade-offs (bridge qubits, time-optimal computation with reaction-time offsets) are used to parallelize circuit segments and minimize total qubit-seconds.

title: GSplit: Scaling Graph Neural Network Training on Large Graphs via Probabilistic Splitting
problem: Mini-batch GNN training with data parallelism causes significant redundant feature loading and computation because the same graph vertices appear in multiple GPU micro-batches, limiting scalability to large graphs.
method: Split parallelism: each mini-batch is sampled once and non-overlappingly partitioned (split) on-the-fly among GPUs using an offline probabilistic splitting algorithm. The offline phase uses pre-sampling to weight graph vertices and edges by expected sampling frequency, then applies weighted min-edge-cut partitioning (METIS) to find a global vertex-to-GPU assignment. Online splitting maps each sampled vertex to its pre-assigned GPU in constant time. Inter-GPU feature shuffles at each GNN layer exchange only required features.
